query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration, intermediate-temperature annealing treatment (~700°C for a few minutes) followed by rapid quenching applied to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce the in situ formation of an ultrathin, coherent, ductile interfacial precipitate along the lamellar boundaries, which will serve as a dislocation sink to alleviate pile-ups, reduce local stress concentrations, and thereby overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness without compromising strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
generation.intervention: Apply a short-duration annealing treatment at approximately 700°C for several minutes, immediately followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing and typical operating conditions for high-strength applications.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrathin, coherent ductile interfacial precipitate (or interphase) that forms along the existing lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The ductile interfacial phase acts as a dislocation sink, absorbing and deflecting dislocations to reduce pile-ups at the internal boundaries, thus decreasing local stress concentrations and mitigating microcrack initiation during straining.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit improved tensile ductility (higher strain-to-failure) and maintain or even enhance its strength compared to the untreated material.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy shows low room-temperature ductility due to dislocation pile-ups at sharp, stress-concentrating lamellar boundaries, leading to microcracking and premature failure.
generation.boundary: The success of the intervention depends on precisely controlling the annealing temperature and time to form a continuous, coherent interfacial phase without coarsening the lamellar microstructure; deviations might either not form the ductile phase or degrade the overall architecture.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing window and the quantitative improvement in ductility (and retention of strength) remain to be determined, as the balance between interfacial precipitation and microstructural coarsening is sensitive to treatment conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the proposed annealing treatment (around 700°C for a few minutes with rapid quenching) and retain a control set with no treatment. Perform systematic room-temperature tensile tests on both sets while characterizing the microstructure using TEM and HAADF-STEM to assess the presence and continuity of the ductile interfacial phase.
measurements: Quantitative measurement of tensile yield strength and strain-to-failure
Microscopic imaging of internal interfaces to detect the ductile interlayer formation
Assessment of dislocation distribution and evidence of pile-ups via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility (i.e., increased strain-to-failure) or if the tensile strength is reduced relative to the control, or if microstructural analyses fail to show the formation of a coherent ductile interfacial phase alleviating dislocation pile-ups, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

decision.trend: Over the past decade, researchers working on high‐entropy alloys have moved from altering the bulk lamellar spacing and overall phase morphology (often via cold deformation or conventional heat treatments) to more refined strategies that tailor the interfaces between phases. Early attempts improved ductility by refining the microstructure, but these often compromised strength. More recently, work such as that in PMC10213035 has demonstrated that a step‐wise thermo‐mechanical process, which induces coherent precipitation at internal boundaries, can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility. These studies reveal that converting the typically ‘sharp’ and stress‐concentrating internal interfaces into engineered, ductile interlayers that can absorb or deflect dislocations is key. However, despite progress, the specific challenge of mitigating dislocation pile‐ups at the lamellar colony boundaries without altering the dual‐phase architecture remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: How to directly modify the internal lamellar colony interfaces so that they can accommodate dislocation flux and relieve local stress concentrations – and thus avoid microcracking – while preserving the high-strength dual-phase lamellar architecture remains open. In other words, while interfacial engineering via controlled precipitation has been explored, a single, straightforward intervention that forms a continuous, ductile interphase at these critical boundaries is yet to be realized.
decision.lever: Apply a short-duration, intermediate-temperature annealing treatment (for example, around 700°C for a few minutes) followed by rapid quenching to promote the in situ formation of an ultrathin, coherent and ductile interfacial phase along the lamellar boundaries.
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the evolving trend of using thermomechanical treatments to tailor interfaces. By inducing a controlled, interfacial precipitation reaction, the treatment creates a ductile interlayer that can act as a dislocation sink—thereby alleviating local stress concentrations from pile-ups—while preserving or even enhancing the overall strength. Such an intervention addresses the identified root cause of brittle failure and aligns with the need for a single processing step that maintains the dual-phase colony architecture under room-temperature tensile conditions.
